newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/yen pullback eases U.S. automakers' pain.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen pullback eases U.S. automakers' pain.

text.p: The dollar's sharp drop against the yen has manufacturers of U.S. cars smiling, but not yet relaxing.
Having endured costly market-share losses to Japanese competitors in recent months, domestic producers expect the dollar's ricochet from a 57-month high versus the yen to help reverse the trend.
"We're starting to get to a range that's more reflective of the fundamentals of the Japanese economy," said Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers Association (AAMA).

The dollar touched 111.55 yen in Tokyo trading Wednesday, down 13 percent from a peak of 127.47 on May 1. The one-month collapse effectively ended a two-year rally from 79.75 yen, a post-World War II low.
"I'm amazed it's happened so quickly," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington think-tank.
"If the dollar stays at these levels or goes a little lower, most (U.S. manufacturers) will be pretty happy. Certainly, this is a heck of a lot better than 127," he added.
Many manufacturing leaders have called 110 yen a fair level for the dollar, though some would obviously prefer a bit more competitive advantage.
"My personal view is it should be more in the 95-105 range, but we're heading in the right direction," Card said.
Trade data, especially in the auto sector, show a clear trend in favor of Japanese producers in recent months.
U.S. automaker share of domestic light vehicle sales fell to 72 percent in the first five months of 1997 from 74.3 percent in the same period in 1996, according to the AAMA.
Japan's share of the U.S. market rose to 23.8 percent from 21.9 percent over the same period.
In addition, Japan's motor vehicle exports to the United States rose 24.1 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 versus the fourth quarter of 1995.
"That's not accomplished with product built in North America, but with product that they ship from Japan, so it's directly yen-related," Card said.

In Japan, where the average vehicle sells for two million yen, the return in dollars for U.S. exporters had fallen to $16,000 at a dollar/yen rate of 125, compared to $20,000 at 100 and $25,000 at 80.
"Excessive yen weakness challenges our ability to compete in their market and creates an unlevel playing field in the U.S. market," Card said.
Yet experts said it will take several months before the trade figures begin to reflect the reversal in the currency markets.
"The rest of this year looks bad. We really won't see any impact from a trade perspective until late 1997 or 1998," said Chimerine.
In addition, the yen's recent vigor could prove fleeting, with much higher interest rates and stronger economic growth in the United States still drawing capital away from Japan.

"Before we get too excited about the dollar's decline, we ought to recognize it's a reversal of an increase, about which people were getting excited not long ago," said Marvin Kosters, an economist at the American Enterprise Institute think-tank.
A break of 110.50 yen could trigger a wave of loss-cut and options-linked dollar selling, a trader at a trust bank said.
However, if the dollar were to fall below 110.00 yen, this would fuel worries about the possibility of intervention by financial authorities, dealers said.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters on Wednesday that Japan would take appropriate and timely measures against excessive currency moves.
"If Japanese government officials continue to express worries about the recent yen rise, that could eventually help the market stabilise," said the city bank trader.
